terms.definition: The physical element of a crime: the conduct (an act or an omission), in the required circumstances, and for a result crime the prohibited consequence.
terms.examiner: The conduct must be voluntary (Hill v Baxter). In a scenario, deal with the actus reus before the mens rea.

terms.definition: A failure to act. There is no liability for an omission unless the defendant was under a legal duty to act.
terms.examiner: Know the duty situations with a case each: contract (Pittwood), relationship (Gibbins and Proctor), voluntary assumption of care (Stone and Dobinson), creating a dangerous situation (Miller), public office (Dytham).

terms.definition: The "but for" test: the consequence would not have happened but for the defendant's conduct.
terms.examiner: White (1910) is the case where the test was not met; Pagett is one where it was. Apply the test to the facts in one sentence, then move to legal causation.

terms.definition: The defendant's conduct must be an operating and substantial cause of the consequence, meaning more than a minimal contribution.
terms.examiner: Smith (1959) for "operating and substantial"; Kimsey for more than a slight or trifling link. It need not be the only cause.

terms.definition: A new intervening act that breaks the chain of causation: the act of a third party, the victim's own act, or a natural and unforeseeable event.
terms.examiner: Medical treatment rarely breaks the chain (Smith, Cheshire; contrast Jordan). A victim's escape breaks it only if it was so "daft" as to be unforeseeable (Roberts, Williams).

terms.definition: The defendant must take the victim as they find them, so is liable for the full harm even if a characteristic of the victim made it worse.
terms.examiner: Blaue: the victim's refusal of a blood transfusion on religious grounds did not break the chain.

terms.definition: The consequence is the defendant's aim or purpose.
terms.examiner: Mohan (1975): a decision to bring about the consequence. Do not discuss oblique intention when the facts show a clear aim.

terms.definition: The consequence was not the defendant's aim, but it was a virtual certainty as a result of their actions and they appreciated that.
terms.examiner: Woollin (1998). Matthews and Alleyne: foresight of virtual certainty is evidence from which the jury may find intention, not intention itself.

terms.definition: The defendant foresaw a risk of the consequence and went on to take it unreasonably.
terms.examiner: Cunningham (1957), confirmed in R v G (2003). It is enough for assault, battery, s47 and s20; it is not enough for s18 or murder.

terms.definition: Mens rea aimed at one victim is transferred to the unintended victim of the same type of offence.
terms.examiner: Latimer. It does not transfer between different types of offence: Pembliton (person to property).
